subject: mathematics_2a
question_text: If n is a positive integer, show that (p + iq)^(1/n) + (p − iq)^(1/n) = 2(p² + q²)^(1/2n) cos((1/n) Tan⁻¹(q/p)).

mark_split.label: Take the 1/n power by De Moivre's theorem

recall_prompt: Say how you would prove this — how you write p + iq in mod-amp form, what a 1/n power does to r and to θ, and how the two roots combine.
insider_note: Same method as the (1 + i)ⁿ questions, but with letters and a fractional power. The exponent on the modulus is 1/2n, not 1/n: the square root inside r is easy to forget.

steps.label: Mod-amp form of p + iq
steps.margin_note: First and second marks. With x = p and y = q, r = √(p² + q²) and tan θ = q/p, so θ = Tan⁻¹(q/p). Name θ here; the final answer is written in terms of it.
lines: Let p + iq = x + iy ⇒ x = p, y = q
tan θ = y/x = q/p ⇒ θ = Tan⁻¹(q/p)
∴ p + iq = √(p² + q²) (cos θ + i sin θ),

recall.must_convey: That p + iq is first written in modulus-amplitude form: r = √(p² + q²) and θ = Tan⁻¹(q/p), giving r(cos θ + i sin θ).

steps.why: De Moivre's theorem works only on a number written as cos θ + i sin θ. Pulling out r first is what makes the theorem usable, so this line is the method, not a preliminary.
common_mistakes: Writing r = p² + q² without the square root.
Writing θ = Tan⁻¹(p/q), upside down; tan θ is y over x, so q over p.
Forgetting to name θ, which makes the final answer impossible to write.

steps.label: Take the 1/n power by De Moivre
steps.margin_note: Third and fourth marks. A 1/n power divides the angle, so the cosine and the sine take θ/n. The modulus is (p² + q²) to the power 1/2 raised again to 1/n, so its exponent is 1/2n and not 1/n.

recall.must_convey: That De Moivre's theorem is applied with the power 1/n: r becomes (p² + q²) to the 1/2n and the angle becomes θ/n, giving equation (1).
accept: apply De Moivre with power one by n so the angle becomes theta by n and r becomes p squared plus q squared to the one by two n
the one by n power divides the angle by n and the modulus is raised to one by two n
by De Moivre cos theta plus i sin theta to the one by n is cos theta by n plus i sin theta by n
De Moivre lo power one by n pettite angle theta by n avuthundi
one value of the nth root is r to the one by n times cis theta by n

steps.why: De Moivre's theorem with a fractional power gives ONE of the n values of the root, the one whose angle is θ/n. The square root inside r is why the modulus ends with exponent 1/2n: (1/2) times (1/n).
common_mistakes: Writing the modulus power as 1/n instead of 1/2n; the square root contributes the extra 1/2.
Multiplying the angle by n instead of dividing it by n.
Claiming this is the only nth root; it is one value, which is all the question asks for.

steps.label: The conjugate root
steps.margin_note: Fifth mark. p − iq is the conjugate of p + iq, so this root carries the same modulus factor with the sine sign reversed. Label it (2); nothing is recomputed.

recall.must_convey: That the conjugate number is treated in the same way and gives (p² + q²) to the 1/2n times (cos(θ/n) − i sin(θ/n)), called equation (2), with the sign of the sine term changed.
accept: similarly the conjugate gives the same thing with minus i sin, that is equation two
do the same for the conjugate and only the sign of the sine changes
the second bracket is the conjugate so its power is (p² + q²) to the 1/2n times (cos(θ/n) − i sin(θ/n))

steps.why: The second number is the conjugate of the first, so it has the same r and the angle −θ. Nothing new has to be computed; only the sign of the sine changes.
common_mistakes: Changing the sign of the cosine as well as the sine.
Recomputing r and θ from scratch and losing time.
Writing equation (2) without the minus sign, so nothing cancels in the next step.

steps.label: Add (1) and (2)
steps.margin_note: Sixth and seventh marks. Adding (1) and (2) cancels the i sin terms and doubles the cosine: 2(p² + q²) to the power 1/2n, times cos(θ/n). Replace θ by Tan⁻¹(q/p), which is the form the question asks for.

recall.must_convey: That equations (1) and (2) are added, the i sin terms cancel, and the result is 2 times (p² + q²) to the 1/2n times cos of (1/n) Tan⁻¹(q/p).
accept: add one and two, the i sin terms cancel and we get 2 times (p² + q²) to the 1/2n times cos of (1/n) Tan⁻¹(q/p)
adding the two equations the sine parts cancel leaving two times the cosine
one plus two gives two cos and the final answer is 2 times (p² + q²) to the 1/2n times cos of (1/n) Tan⁻¹(q/p)

the imaginary parts cancel on adding and the answer is two to the n plus one times cos

steps.why: The two roots are conjugates, so their sum is twice the real part; adding removes the i sin terms and leaves the cosine. The book's last line prints the second bracket as (p − q) with the i missing; the card writes (p − iq).
common_mistakes: Leaving θ in the answer instead of replacing it by Tan⁻¹(q/p), which the question asks for.
Subtracting instead of adding, which leaves 2i sin instead of 2 cos.
Dropping the factor (p² + q²) to the 1/2n.
